thesis: Goldman has de-rated 22.4% from its 120-day high of 1153.99 to 895.32 while the S&P 500 sits 0.39% from its own high — a 15-point underperformance versus SPY in one month (GS -12.2%, SPY +2.74%) and 8.4 points versus XLF. The identifiable cause is a deferral rather than an impairment: equity-capital-markets pipeline slipped when OpenAI delayed its IPO, which pushes advisory and underwriting fees into 2027 instead of destroying them, and that is the revenue line most exposed to a calendar. Meanwhile the stock has stopped going down — the 120-day low of 868.52 printed 2026-10-07, followed by higher lows at 876.77 and 878.86 and a Friday close of 895.32 near the session high of 899.67. The trade is that Tuesday's print re-anchors the name to earnings power rather than to deal-calendar sentiment, and the 50-day at 989.93 is the first level the September de-rating has to give back.
key_risk: Earnings is a binary event two sessions away and this is a long into it, which is why the entry waits for the reaction instead of anticipating it. Worse, September CPI prints the following morning: the whole bank complex has been sold on the fear of additional Fed hikes with TLT within 2% of its 120-day low, so a hot CPI re-fires exactly the driver that caused the drawdown and would hit a one-day-old position. The stop at 857 sits below the 868.52 low because a new low after the print falsifies the basing structure the entry depends on.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that this is a laggard and the measurement says so without ambiguity: GS underperforms SPY on every window (1m -12.2%, 3m -14.4%, 6m -1.37%) and underperforms even the lagging XLF by 8-12 points. Buying the weakest name in the weakest sector while the index makes highs is a bet against the only trend the tape is actually expressing. There is no insider confirmation either — zero open-market purchases against 21 sales over six months. If the bank drawdown is an early credit signal rather than a deal-calendar wobble, a 22% fall is the start and not the opportunity, and the IPO-delay story is a comfortable narrative wrapped around a rate problem.

thesis: Steel equities are in an upgrade cycle while the group still trades below its summer levels, and Steel Dynamics is the profitable way to own it. Analyst revisions have turned measurably positive across the complex — Wells Fargo moved Cleveland-Cliffs to Overweight explicitly citing steel pricing power, with target raises from GLJ and JPMorgan alongside — and realised pricing is confirming it, with CLF's average selling price at 1,124 dollars per net ton in Q2 against 1,048 in Q1. STLD itself has beaten consensus in three of its last four quarters and earns 3.81 a share against CLF's four straight losses, so the same pricing leverage arrives on an income statement that is already in profit. The chart has stopped breaking down: the 120-day low of 219.10 printed 2026-10-01, the pullback since held a higher low at 232.97, and the 241.36 50-day plus the 245.185 high of 10-05 form one overhead shelf that a Q3 print on better pricing is the natural thing to clear.
key_risk: The entry sits above the market and only triggers on strength, so the real risk is not a wrong level but a wrong regime: steel is a cyclical levered to industrial demand, and the macro read elsewhere in this run is hostile to cyclicals — IWM is 8.6% off its high and below its 50-day, XLI is 10.06% off its high, and the bank complex is in correction on fear of additional Fed hikes. If higher-for-longer breaks industrial demand, a pricing-driven beat will be sold rather than bought. Entering before a 10-19 print also means an earnings gap is live, which is why the plan trims half into it instead of holding through.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that the pricing evidence I am leaning on is CLF's, not STLD's: the 1,124-per-ton figure and the Wells Fargo upgrade are a Cleveland-Cliffs datapoint and a Cleveland-Cliffs rating, and I am extending them across the group. STLD's own revision signal is thin — bullish share 63.6%, up only 1.7 points, with one sell rating still outstanding — and there is no insider confirmation at all, zero open-market purchases against 13 sales. A stronger version of the bear case: STLD is 17.44% off its high and below its 50-day for a reason, and an upgrade cycle driven by sell-side targets rather than by orders is the weakest kind of catalyst.

Price has already stopped falling — the 120-day low of 345.23 is well behind it, the stock is above its 20-day at 374.92, and Friday it traded up to 387.52 on a 2.25% day. What it has not done is reclaim the 389.18 50-day, which has capped every attempt since 2026-09-18. The trade is that a third consecutive beat is the thing that converts an improving estimate trend into a reclaimed 50-day, and that managed care re-rates off a depressed base rather than needing the whole 461 high back.
key_risk: The stop at 367.00 is the honest weak point of this idea and I am naming it rather than hiding it: at 2.54 ATR it clears the config floor comfortably, but it sits ABOVE the 2026-10-01 swing low of 362.60 and only just below the 368.50 low of 10-08. A routine retest of the base that the stock has traded in all month would stop this out without the thesis being wrong. Placing the stop properly below 362.60 widens risk to 28.00 and drops reward-to-risk to 1.80, which fails — so this idea passes on the ATR test while being genuinely vulnerable on the structural one. Beyond that: managed care carries policy and medical-cost-trend risk that no chart describes, a Q3 estimate of 4.19 against a Q2 actual of 6.38 shows how lumpy the cost seasonality is, and there are zero insider open-market buys against 3 sales.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that two huge beats have already happened and the stock fell anyway — which is evidence the market does not believe the earnings are the issue. If UNH is 17.8% off its high despite a 28.8% beat, then the de-rating is about medical cost trend, Medicare Advantage rate pressure or regulatory overhang, and a third beat will be discounted the same way the first two were. On that reading the improving sell-side revision trend is the lagging indicator and the price is the leading one. The entry requirement is the answer to this, imperfectly: by demanding a reclaim of 389.18 after the print, the trade refuses to take a view on the print at all and only pays up once the market itself has re-rated the name. The cost of that discipline is that in the bear case there is no fill and no trade, which is the correct outcome.

thesis: Morgan Stanley has beaten consensus in four consecutive quarters — by 14.11%, 10.92%, 6.78% and 29.27% — and sell-side positioning is the one thing in the bank complex actually improving, with bullish share up 4.4 points to 60.6% while BAC deteriorated 3.5 points and GS sat flat at 46.9%. The stock is nonetheless 18.18% below its 120-day high of 232.25, because the whole group has been marked down on rate fear and because the OpenAI IPO delay pushed equity-capital-markets fees into 2027. That is a deferral of revenue, not a loss of it, and it lands on the business line most sensitive to a calendar. Price has already stopped making lows: the 120-day low of 182.47 printed 2026-10-01 and has been followed by a sequence of higher lows at 185.22, 186.15 and 187.05. The trade is that Q3 lands on the same morning the macro question is answered, and a fifth straight beat into a cleared CPI is what takes the stock back through the 195.99 20-day toward the 207.33 50-day.
key_risk: This and the GS idea in the same report are ONE bet, not two — both are capital-markets banks hit by the same ECM-deferral story and the same rate fear, so they will succeed or fail together. They are sized at 1.5% each for that reason; treat the pair as a single 3% position and do not size them independently. Beyond the correlation: a hot September CPI on the morning of 10-14 re-fires exactly the driver that caused this drawdown, and because it prints alongside the earnings the two cannot be separated — a good quarter can be entirely overwhelmed by the macro number, and the 193.14 trigger would simply never fire. There is also no insider confirmation at all: zero open-market purchases against 17 sales in six months.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that four straight beats have already happened and the stock is still 18% off its high, which says the market is not pricing MS off its earnings at all — it is pricing the rate path and the deal calendar, neither of which a Q3 beat settles. On that reading the improving sell-side revision trend is just analysts marking to a print they can forecast while the thing that actually matters is unforecastable. The second objection is mine against myself: I chose MS over BAC on revision direction, but BAC also beat four of four and has the tidier chart target, and the honest answer is that the revision screen is a thin reed to pick between two good setups. The entry condition is the partial answer to both — requiring a reclaim of 193.14 after both events means the trade only pays up once the market has resolved the questions the thesis cannot.
